items.q: What software do I need to start selling physical products online?
items.a: At minimum, an ecommerce platform to take payment and ship orders. Shopify's Basic plan costs $39 a month and covers a solo founder completely: hosting, a checkout, discount codes, abandoned-cart recovery and automatic sales tax, all in one bill, with no separate hosting or security patching to manage. Everything else on this page is worth adding once the store has real traffic, not before it. Email and SMS marketing, through a tool such as Klaviyo, pays for itself once there are actual orders and abandoned carts to follow up on, and a workspace such as Notion for supplier contacts and SOPs matters more once the catalog grows past a size one person can remember. A brand testing its first product can launch on the platform alone and add the rest as it sells.

items.q: Is WooCommerce cheaper than Shopify for a small store?
items.a: On the platform bill alone, yes: WooCommerce's real cost for a solo seller is about $25 a month, almost all of it hosting, against Shopify's $39 for the Basic plan, since the WooCommerce plugin itself is free. That comparison only holds if you're comfortable running WordPress yourself, though. WooCommerce doesn't include hosting, security updates or plugin maintenance the way Shopify's plan does, so a founder with no WordPress experience often spends more time than the monthly saving is worth. WooCommerce tends to be the better deal specifically for a brand that already runs a WordPress site, since it is adding a store to infrastructure it pays for anyway, or for one that wants full control of its checkout code and no share of revenue taken by the platform. For a brand starting from nothing, the maintenance is the real cost to weigh against the sticker price.

items.q: How much does a full software stack cost for a 5-person store team?
items.a: Around $315 a month for the three tools on this page: Shopify's Grow plan at $105 a month for up to five staff accounts, Klaviyo at $150 a month for a list of about 10,000 active profiles, and Notion at $60 a month for five seats. That figure assumes Shopify Payments, so no added transaction fee, a list that fits Klaviyo's 10,000-profile tier, and no paid add-ons on either tool. It doesn't include card-processing fees, which every platform charges regardless of which one you pick, or any apps layered on top. A team that's still under five staff logins, or has a smaller email list, pays less on each layer; the biggest lever on this total as the business grows is usually the email and SMS tool's list size, not the ecommerce plan.

items.q: Do I need Klaviyo, or can I use my store platform's built-in email tools?
items.a: Shopify's own Shopify Messaging includes 10,000 marketing emails a month free on every paid plan, so a brand testing its first product can start there at no extra cost. The gap shows up in SMS and in how deeply the tool understands a customer's history: Klaviyo's flows are built around active-profile data synced from ecommerce order and browsing history, with a published SMS rate, while Shopify's own messaging tool is a simpler add-on to the platform rather than a dedicated retention system. A solo founder with a small list can reasonably wait on Klaviyo and use the free included emails first. Once abandoned-cart recovery, back-in-stock alerts and post-purchase flows are worth running as a coordinated system rather than one-off sends, a dedicated tool at $30 a month for a first list of about 1,000 profiles is the point where that upgrade makes sense.

items.q: Do I need a CRM to run an online store?
items.a: Not for a typical direct-to-consumer brand. A CRM such as HubSpot or GoHighLevel is built around a sales pipeline: moving a lead through stages until they sign a contract, which fits a business that closes deals one at a time. A store selling physical products to individual consumers doesn't run that process; its customer relationship data is really an order history and an email list, both of which already live in the ecommerce platform and the email and SMS tool. A brand that also sells wholesale to other businesses, where deals really do move through a pipeline, is the exception, and even then a CRM with built-in automation, such as ActiveCampaign, can cover both the consumer email list and the wholesale pipeline in one subscription rather than adding a third.

items.q: What should a new store buy first?
items.a: The ecommerce platform, and nothing else, until the first sale. Shopify's Basic plan at $39 a month, or WooCommerce if you already run WordPress, covers taking payment, hosting and a working checkout on its own; there is no customer list to email yet, and no catalog complex enough to need a dedicated workspace. Add email and SMS marketing once there are real orders and abandoned carts worth following up on, since that is the tool retention flows are built for. A workspace such as Notion is worth setting up early too, even though it costs nothing at this size, since supplier contacts, packing instructions and a launch checklist are much easier to write down from the start than to reconstruct later. A CRM, a second website and a dedicated SEO platform can all wait well past the first sale.

items.q: When should a growing store move off Shopify's Grow plan?
items.a: When staff logins or shipping needs outgrow it, not before. Grow allows up to five staff accounts and covers third-party carrier-calculated shipping only with yearly billing or an added monthly fee; Advanced, at $399 a month, raises the staff cap to 15 and includes that shipping option outright. A team that's still within five logins and doesn't need live carrier rates has no reason to pay for Advanced early, since Grow's $105-a-month plan already includes unlimited products, hosting and the same checkout and tax features. The upgrade is triggered by a specific limit being hit, staff count most often, rather than by revenue alone; a 15-person team where most staff never need their own Shopify login can, in practice, stay on Grow longer than its size would suggest.
